To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have observed a general derangement of cyclin expression in a number of breast cancer cell lines, and that this derangement is associated with a number of other changes that may be important in the development of cancer.

we observed a number (i.e., 9 of 9) of breast tumor lines to have deranged expression of a large number of cyclins, which we believe may be involved in the loss of growth control in human breast cancer.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular mechanisms of cell cycle regulation, particularly in relation to human cancer.
the molecular mechanisms of cell cycle control in normal vs. cancerous human breast cells.
the role of cyclin expression in cell proliferation and differentiation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
cyclins A and E are the only two cyclins that are amplified in breast cancer.
there is general overexpression of cyclins in breast cancer cells, and that this overexpression is due to gene amplification and increased mRNA stability.
the cyclins are involved in tumorigenesis and that cyclin E amplification and derangement of cyclin expression may be involved in the development of human breast cancer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the cyclin overexpression observed in breast cancer cells is not limited to a single cyclin, and that this overexpression is not a result of a specific genetic change, but rather is a result of a general derangement of the cell cycle machinery.
there is a significant correlation between general cyclin expression and tumorigenesis.
there are general derangements (i.e., overexpression and gene duplication) in cyclin expression and regulation in tumor cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are multiple alterations in cyclin gene expression in breast cancer cells, and this is not limited to the two cyclins previously implicated in cancer.
cyclin overexpression is a general phenomenon in breast cancer cells, and it is a result of both amplification and altered stability of cyclin RNAs, as well as altered expression of proteins.
the cyclin overexpression is not limited to a single cyclin, but is rather general, involving all cyclins.
